from_notes: The Company's monopoly over trade with China and in tea also ended.
x: The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company's remaining monopolies (tea and the China trade); 1813 had kept them.
source: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28; Spectrum Modern India (src/indian-history/spectrum-modern-india.txt) p.537

x: Not true: the 1813 Act did not end the monopoly 'including its tea trade' (tea, opium and the China trade stayed with the Company till 1833). It did allow missionaries and assert Crown sovereignty.

from_notes: Agra Presidency: present UP separated from Bengal Presidency (1834)
x: Under the Charter Act of 1833 the Agra Presidency was created in 1834, taking almost all of present UP out of the Bengal Presidency (renamed North-Western Provinces in 1836).
source: app notes 1:174 sub 3

from_notes: It made the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India
from_notes_src: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28
x: The Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India (Bentinck the first).
source: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28

from_notes: it established a separate Governor-General's legislative council which came to be known as the Indian (Central) Legislative Council
from_notes_src: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28
x: The Charter Act of 1853 first separated the legislative and executive functions and created the Central Legislative Council, a 'mini-Parliament'.
source: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28; PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.2

x: Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against sati (abolished 1829) and for women's rights and education; Vivekananda, Tilak and Sarojini Naidu are not the answer. (Moved to the Ram Mohan Roy row.)
source: general knowledge, not checked

from_notes: The first Law Commission was appointed in India in 1834 under the Charter Act of 1833 and was presided over by Lord Macaulay.
from_notes_src: PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.1
x: The First Law Commission (1834) set up under the Charter Act of 1833 to codify Indian laws was headed by Macaulay.
source: PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.1

from_notes: Macaulay: "The Company is an anomaly but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly" (Commons speech, 1833 Bill)
x: T.B. Macaulay, speaking in the Commons on the 1833 Charter Bill, said: 'The Company is an anomaly but it is part of a system where everything is an anomaly.'
source: app notes 1:174 sub 5

x: The Imperial Legislative Council, set up under the Indian Councils Act of 1861, was British India's legislature from 1861 until 1947.
source: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.29
evidence: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.29: Indian Councils Act 1861 associated Indians with law-making

x: The Charter Act of 1853 renewed the Company's rule with no fixed term, the territories being held 'in trust for Her Majesty' until Parliament provided otherwise. The 1833 Act already used the words 'in trust for His Majesty'.
source: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28; PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.1
evidence: Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28: 1833 – territories held 'in trust for His Majesty, His heirs and successors'; 1853 – retain possession on trust for the Crown
PMF Modern Indian History Part 3 (src/indian-history/pmf-modern-history-03.txt) p.1: 1833 – Indian possessions held in trust for the British Crown
dispute: APPSC 2018 and the app: Charter Act 1853. Laxmikanth and PMF also give the 'in trust' clause in the Charter Act 1833 (Laxmikanth Indian Polity 8th ed. Part 1 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-01.txt) p.28).
